title: Was reading Arpit Bhayani's latest piece and realized something
excerpt: Every database decision you've ever made assumed one thing:
body:
Was reading Arpit Bhayani's latest piece and realize:

Every database decision you've ever made assumed one thing:

The caller is deterministic code. Written by a human. Reviewed by a human. Deployed by a human.

That assumption held for 40 years.
Agents just broke it.

• They generate queries no one has ever seen before.
• They hold connections while the LLM "thinks.
• They write data autonomously and retry when they shouldn't.
• They fail silently. No exception. No alert. Just bad data.

The wild part?
The fixes aren't new technology.
Soft deletes. Idempotency keys. Append-only logs. Least-privilege roles. Query tagging.
We've had these patterns for years.
We just kept saying "we'll get to it.

Agents don't give you that luxury anymore.
Three things I now treat as non-negotiable:
→ Role-per-agent-type with hard statement timeouts at the DB level
→ Separate connection pools agent traffic and human traffic don't mix
→ Schema designed for LLM legibility, not just developer convenience

This isn't a prompting problem.
It's a database design problem.
The database was never designed for this caller.

But the tools to make it safe; Already in the toolbox.

Blog link in the comments 👇

title: The hardest lesson I learned as a Tech Lead wasn't about technology.
excerpt: Early on, I thought my job was: unblock the team, design clean systems, ship fast.
body:
The hardest lesson I learned as a Tech Lead wasn't about technology.

Early on, I thought my job was: unblock the team, design clean systems, ship fast.

Then came a project that changed everything.

We just need this feature quickly.

No specs. No edge cases. Just urgency.

I filled in the blanks myself and shipped exactly what I thought they needed.

Two weeks later:
→ "Can it handle this scenario?"
→ "Why didn't we make this reusable?"
→ "Compliance needs an audit trail.

The code wasn't wrong. The expectations were.

That's when it clicked:

My job isn't to convert vague requirements into code fast. It's to slow down and ask the right questions—especially when everyone wants to rush.

Now:
✓ Ask "who will actually use this?
✓ Demand examples, not assumptions
✓ Document decisions before coding
✓ Protect my team from unclear asks

Clear requirements don't slow you down. They save you from building the wrong thing three times.

#TechLead #Engineering #Leadership

title: I had two engineers on my team.
excerpt: Engineer A always asked why Why are we building this? Is there a simpler way? Sometimes it was annoying.
body:
I had two engineers on my team.

Engineer A always asked why Why are we building this? Is there a simpler way? Sometimes it was annoying.

Engineer B just wanted clear tickets. Give him the requirements, he would build it fast, clean, no drama.

A year ago, I would have said B was my dream engineer.

Now? I’m all in on A.

Here’s why: AI can write code. But AI can’t decide if the code should even exist.

Engineer B just follows instructions. If the spec is wrong, he still builds it. If there’s a better way, he won’t see it. If the feature ships and nobody uses it? He delivered what was asked job done.

Engineer A drives me crazy with questions. But those questions save us weeks:

“Why are we building this instead of fixing the real problem?”
“Can’t we solve this without writing new code?”
“Did we ask users if they actually need this?”

Sometimes we end up building something smaller. Sometimes we don’t build anything at all.

Engineers who just follow tickets are competing with AI. Engineers who understand the problem? They are solving something AI can’t touch.

Not every developer needs to be a product manager. But the ones who think about the problem, not just the ticket? They are the ones you want on your team.

The real power isn’t in typing code it’s in thinking. In asking questions. In challenging.

title: Most performance issues don’t start with failures.
excerpt: They start with queues quietly growing, then databases get slower, threads pile up, and suddenly everyone is “investiga...
body:
Most performance issues don’t start with failures.
They start with queues quietly growing, then databases get slower, threads pile up, and suddenly everyone is “investigating latency”.

Inside Netflix, engineers tackled this with a simple idea and powerful execution:
Adaptive Concurrency Limits, inspired by how TCP manages congestion.

Instead of hard-coding “safe” concurrency numbers (which are wrong the moment you deploy), Netflix lets each service adjust itself based on real signals:

• Watch latency (time taken to complete a request) in real time

• Detect when queuing begins

• Increase or decrease concurrency automatically, just like TCP slows down when packets get delayed

At the core is a surprisingly clean formula:

newLimit = currentLimit × (minRTT / observedRTT)

• minRTT → best observed latency (no queueing)

• observedRTT → current latency under load

If latency rises, concurrency drops.
If latency stays close to the minimum, concurrency grows.
No guesswork, no static thresholds pretending the system is static.
No dashboards arguing about the “right” number.
No config archaeology during incidents.
The service learns its own limits and backs off before the database taps out.

If the network layer cracked this decades ago, our services can too.

excerpt: Researchers found that Antigravity’s AI, Gemini:
body:
⚠️ Google Antigravity IDE has a serious security flaw!

Researchers found that Antigravity’s AI, Gemini:
1. The attack vector – The AI assistant, Gemini, reads integration guides or instructions you give it. Malicious guides can be “poisoned” with hidden instructions to do bad things.

2. Bypassing protections – Even if you have .env files or .gitignore to hide secrets, Gemini can be tricked into ignoring those safeguards.

3. Exfiltration – Once tricked, Gemini can read sensitive files from your workspace and send them to an attacker’s server.

Google’s response They’ve confirmed the risk but haven’t issued a patch yet.

Takeaway: Don’t blindly feed external guides or scripts into Antigravity. Treat them like untrusted code, because Gemini can act on them.

🔐  PSA: Your SSH Key Isn't Doing What You Think It Does

Quick reality check: pushing code over SSH to GitHub doesn't mean your commits are verified. It just means someone with access pushed them.

Here's the fun part: literally anyone can pretend to be you by typing:
```
git config user.name "Your Name
git config user.email "your@email
```
Congratulations, they're now you. Your boss? Also you. That intern? Yep, you again.

Enter: Verified Commits
When you actually sign your commits with GPG or SSH signing keys, GitHub can cryptographically prove:

You wrote it (not your "evil twin")

Nobody messed with it after

Your git history isn't just collaborative fiction

The TL;DR
SSH proves you can push. Signed commits prove you actually wrote the thing.

Even in private repos, teams that care about security, compliance, or not getting blamed for code they didn't write are making this mandatory.

If you haven't set this up yet, it takes like 10 minutes and saves you from awkward "I didn't commit that" conversations later.

title: Verified Communication: The Invisible Trust Layer in Fintech
excerpt: In fintech, trust isn’t just a value, it’s the product.
body:
💳 Verified Communication: The Invisible Trust Layer in Fintech

In fintech, trust isn’t just a value, it’s the product.
Every email sent to a customer (whether an OTP, investment update, or transaction alert) must carry authenticity baked into its code.

That’s where SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and BIMI come together, a technical stack ensuring every message that leaves your domain can be cryptographically verified.

When Gmail shows

“The sender of this email has verified that they own [domain] and the logo in the profile image,”
it means the system behind that message has passed all layers of domain authentication and brand validation.

Under the hood:

1. SPF checks that the mail server is authorized to send on behalf of your domain.
2. DKIM signs the message with a private key so recipients can verify it hasn’t been altered.
3. DMARC enforces a policy — rejecting or quarantining anything that fails these checks.
4. BIMI adds your verified brand logo, backed by a Verified Mark Certificate (VMC).

Together, they turn a simple email into a cryptographically trusted communication channel.

In fintech, this isn’t cosmetic; it’s a risk control layer.
It stops phishing look-alikes, protects transactional integrity, and ensures customers never hesitate to click a legitimate message.

When customers see an “unknown sender”, they pause.
When they see a verified sender with your logo, they act, because trust has been engineered into the message itself.

The takeaway:

Verified communication isn’t a marketing feature.
It’s a security product every fintech should be shipping by default.

title: RAG vs Fine-tuning
excerpt: When it comes to adapting Large Language Models to new tasks, two approaches dominate: RAG and Fine-tuning. Both enhance model performance for domain-specific use cases, but their architectural differences matter.
body:
RAG vs Fine-tuning

When it comes to adapting Large Language Models to new tasks, two approaches dominate: RAG and Fine-tuning. Both enhance model performance for domain-specific use cases, but their architectural differences matter.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
Runtime knowledge retrieval through vector embeddings and semantic search. External knowledge base remains separate from model weights updating data doesn't require retraining. High traceability with citable sources, ideal for dynamic environments where information changes frequently.

Fine-tuning
Supervised learning that updates model parameters with domain specific datasets. Knowledge is internalized into weights no external retrieval at inference. Better for specialized tasks requiring consistent output formats and improved response latency.

Technical tradeoffs:
• Data freshness: RAG pulls real-time data; fine-tuning is static post-training
• Compute: RAG requires vector DB + orchestration; fine-tuning needs GPU clusters and ML expertise
• Scalability: RAG updates in minutes; fine-tuning requires complete retraining cycles.

Many production systems use hybrid approaches fine-tuned models for task-specific behavior combined with RAG for up-to-date context injection.

For your domain: Do you optimize for knowledge recency (RAG) or embedded expertise (Fine-tuning)?

title: Are remote-first companies setting up young employees to fail?
excerpt: I recently came across a newsletter where 100CEOs shared their thoughts on this exact question and a few responses rea...
body:
Are remote-first companies setting up young employees to fail?
I recently came across a newsletter where 100CEOs shared their thoughts on this exact question and a few responses really stuck with me.

When I started my career, I learned by osmosis: overhearing senior engineers solve problems, getting pulled into impromptu whiteboard sessions, or just chatting over coffee about architecture choices. None of that was scheduled — but that’s where the real growth happened.

Steven Bartlett (FlightStory, Thirdweb) put it well: “Early in your career, work often becomes your community. The mentorship, friendships, and sense of belonging are hard to replace on Zoom.”

Mark Bailie (Compare the Market) said: “Trust isn’t built on video calls. The biggest career accelerators come from face-to-face moments that aren’t in your diary.”

Codie Sanchez (Contrarian Thinking) added: “You miss the osmosis that happens around successful people. The most valuable opportunities don’t happen on Zoom.”

And Nicola Kilner (DECIEM) reminded us that with AI taking over many tasks, people skills and emotional intelligence both best developed in person will only become more valuable.

I’m a huge believer in flexibility and autonomy. But I also think we underestimate how much early-career professionals gain from being physically present the small cues, the informal feedback, the energy of building together.

If I were starting out today, I’d want at least part of my week in an environment where I could observe, connect, and learn.

title: Lazy vs Eager Transformations in Kotlin — Who Works Smarter?
excerpt: When working with data transformations in Kotlin, you often face a choice between two styles: Collections or Sequences.
body:
Lazy vs Eager Transformations in Kotlin — Who Works Smarter?

When working with data transformations in Kotlin, you often face a choice between two styles: Collections or Sequences.
They both work with Lists, Sets, and other iterables — but their approach under the hood is quite different.

Collections
Collections like List, Set, Map apply each transformation (map(), filter(), etc.) immediately.
Each step creates a brand-new collection.

✔️ Best suited for small datasets or a couple of transformations
⚠️ Can become inefficient with longer chains, as each step allocates memory for a new intermediate collection

Sequences
Sequences delay execution. Transformations like map() and filter() don’t do anything until a terminal operation like toList() or count() is called.
✔️ Great for large datasets, long transformation chains, or even infinite streams
⚠️ Slight overhead for small datasets — and once evaluated, the sequence is consumed.

Clean Code tip: Write clean commit messages It’s the best tool to document the reason for change in your code.

Here are 5 tips on how I write commits:

1. Explain the WHY
❌ Add endpoint
✅ Add endpoint to enable users to download purchase history

2. Summarize WHAT the commit does, not HOW it does it:
❌ Changed the button color by updating CSS file
✅ Update primary button color for better contrast

3. Use present tense with imperative mood
❌ I have removed
✅ Remove ...

4. Add link reference to the actual work item
❌ Fix login bug when user is inactive
✅ ab34Dc: Fix login bug when user is inactive

5. Don’t include file names - they are in the Git details
❌ Update dependencies in package.json
✅ Update dependencies to address security vulnerabilities

Clean commit messages are part of internal software quality.

title: The Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) principle isn't just about avoiding duplicate code.
excerpt: If two similar pieces of code represent different business logic, they may need to change for different reasons and at different times. Forcing them to be the same can create problems.
body:
The Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) principle isn't just about avoiding duplicate code.

If two similar pieces of code represent different business logic, they may need to change for different reasons and at different times. Forcing them to be the same can create problems.

However, if two pieces of code represent the same idea or knowledge, they should always change together. In this case, removing duplication makes sense.

DRY is about avoiding repeated knowledge, not just repeated code.

Just a #thought  💭
